Main.dc.html.title: A99 #365 — the order in your screenshot

nA.text:
THE SAME ORDER YOU SCREENSHOTTED

One line item, and today it takes 1103 × 717. Here it is 680 × 446 — a bit over a third of the area.

Eleven blocks of prose are gone. What they said is now a mark, a chip or a figure: the supplier state is a chip, the stage is a position, the margin is a meter against your floor.

The red button is the act you came for. It used to sit on "Send the client an update".

nB.text:
FIVE LINES, ONE OF THEM SHORT

The mark carries what a sentence used to. Filled with a tick: it is here. Amber with a bar: less came than was asked for. Hollow: still with a supplier, or not picked yet.

Three shapes as well as three grounds, so it never rests on colour alone.

Still quieter than today's dialog holding a single line.

nC.text:
WHAT IS NOT READ EVERY TIME

"How it got here" opens in place. Today it is always open, above the money, on every order — five rows of history you did not ask for.

The two empty photo frames are gone. Photos appear as thumbnails when there are some, and taking one lives in the "···" beside the title. When there are none, they cost nothing.

nD.text:
ONE-HANDED

52px rows, 48px buttons, the two acts the width of the screen.

Nothing had to be dropped to fit: none of what survived was a paragraph to begin with.

n2.text:
Today there is no ··· at all. Three of these six acts have no button anywhere on the screen — step back, edit the lines, photos — and two more are ghost buttons in the footer, competing with the act you came for.

Six acts behind one mark, with the three that MOVE the order grouped away from the three that do not.

n3.text:
The decision is which of two numbers to bill, and today both are inside a sentence: “Billing what was picked makes this order 2,243,000 UGX, down from 2,321,000 UGX.”

So show the two numbers and let one be picked. The button then says what it will do — “Bill 1 Roll” — instead of “Supplied in full anyway” sitting beside “Bill for what was picked”, which are the same shape and opposite meanings.

n4.text:
A buying round is a set of PLACES somebody drives to, so the object on the screen should be the place.

One card per stop, holding everything that stop needs: what it costs to carry, what is on it, whether anybody has been sent, and the one act.

That removes three things at once — the supplier repeated on every row, the amber band about lines nobody is buying, and the footer sentence about what this dialog does not do. Each card says its own state instead.

n5.text:
A delivery round is the same object as a buying round, pointed the other way: a set of PLACES, with orders on each and somebody carrying them. So it gets the same card, and the two screens become one thing to learn.

Gone with the table: the destination repeated on every row under a head that already names it, four identical “Delivered” buttons, and twenty-two words of footer saying what marking delivered does and that an empty run closes itself — both true every time, news never.

The run with no place on file is not a run yet, so it wears an amber mark and its act is to fix that.

t6.text: Two other ways to draw it

n6.text:
GOODS FIRST — the thing being tracked is stuff on a shelf, so the QUANTITY is the biggest element on the screen and each line is a tile you could read at arm's length. “1 of 2 Roll” tells the whole short story without a sentence anywhere.

It costs height: five lines take 690px where the table takes 620. Worth it on an order somebody walks around the yard with; wasteful on a two-line one.

THE JOURNEY — the stage track and “how it got here” are the same object seen twice, so draw it once, down the side. The history stops being a section, and the supplier chip sits at the stage where it is true rather than floating above everything.

It costs width: 210px of the dialog is the spine, which is generous for five words.

Neither is better than the one on the canvas at every size. Goods-first wins on long orders, the journey wins on short ones, and the flat one wins on neither and loses on neither.
